folds.subject: slavery
folds.why: Slavery is a distinct topic with its own claims about local complicity, abolition, and withdrawal of support.

groups.why: Both express the case for less government, with s1 stating the endpoint of s0's argument.
Both say government fails to secure freedom; s12 explains that people accomplish what government does not.
s17 lists examples of the bodily service that s16 describes.
Both reject association with the government; s20 gives the decisive reason.
These sentences develop one claim: voting treats moral questions like a game, so its obligation is limited to expediency.
Each asks why government fails to enable reform and heed criticism.
s43 develops s42's point that the tax-gatherer is a neighbor and human agent, not merely an instrument.
Both describe government confronting a person through physical force rather than moral or intellectual authority.
Both ground governmental authority in the governed person's consent; s68 states the limit on that authority.
Both ask whether government can progress beyond democracy toward fuller recognition of human rights.
s73 imagines the just state whose defining principle s72 states.
Both ask whether conscience, rather than legislators or majorities, should decide questions of right and wrong.
Both put moral duty before political subjection; s78 states the individual's governing obligation.
s86 restates the costly duty to restore what was unjustly taken, even at the risk of one's life.
These sentences distinguish between having to solve every wrong and having to avoid supporting one.
s100 gives examples of the revolutionary changes that principled action produces.
s108's refusal to pay taxes is the example that s109 identifies as a peaceable revolution.
s112 gives the personal example behind s111's claim that disobedience costs less than obedience.
Both describe withdrawing allegiance from the State; s114 restates that stance as a quiet declaration of war.
s118 illustrates how respect for law can make people agents of injustice.
s122 explains why people follow s121's strategy of waiting for majority reform.
Both locate responsibility for distant oppression in local people who cooperate with it.
s129 summarizes the inactivity of people whose opposition to slavery and war is described in s128.
s131 states the consequence of s130's claim that majority abolition will come only when little slavery remains.
Both urge abolitionists to withdraw support without waiting for a majority; s134 reinforces the basis for acting.
s138 explains the slow improvement described in s137: people wait for others to remedy the evil.
s141 explains why voting for the right is only a weak expression of support, not action for it.
These sentences describe the respectable voter's retreat into an available candidate and the resulting loss of political integrity.
s148 gives an example of pursuing one's own life while benefiting from another person's burden.
s164's acorn and chestnut illustrate s165's claim that a person dies if unable to live according to their nature.
